title: Mental Health — Psychosis II: Hallucinations, Delusions, Safety & Adherence (Set 22)
subtitle: Phase-2 depth: command-hallucination safety assessment, prioritization, anosognosia and adherence (including LAIs), recognizing relapse/decompensation, responding to grandiose/somatic delusions, managing negative symptoms, distinguishing akathisia from agitation, concrete communication, and coping strategies
scenario: Applying safe, reality-based care for clients experiencing psychosis: assessing command hallucinations for safety, responding to different delusion types without arguing, supporting medication adherence and recognizing relapse, and communicating clearly with clients who think concretely.

steps.q: Negative symptoms of schizophrenia (such as flat affect, low motivation, and social withdrawal) are important to recognize because they:

opts.text: Are part of the illness and are often mistaken for laziness or depression
opts.rat: Negative symptoms reflect the disorder, not a character flaw; misreading them as laziness leads to unfair judgment and missed care needs.

opts.text: Mean the client is simply choosing to be lazy
opts.rat: Negative symptoms are part of the illness, not a deliberate choice.

opts.text: Are the same as hallucinations
opts.rat: Hallucinations are positive symptoms; withdrawal and flat affect are negative symptoms.

opts.text: Should be ignored as unimportant
opts.rat: Negative symptoms significantly affect functioning and are addressed, not ignored.

steps.q: A client reports hearing voices. To assess for safety, the MOST important question is:

opts.text: 'Are the voices telling you to hurt yourself or someone else, and can you resist them?'
opts.rat: Screening for command hallucinations to harm self/others—and the client's ability to resist—identifies an immediate safety risk.

opts.text: 'What color do you think the voices are?'
opts.rat: This does not assess safety or command content.

opts.text: 'Why are you making up these voices?'
opts.rat: This is accusatory and does not assess safety; the experience is real to the client.

opts.text: 'Have you told your family how silly this is?'
opts.rat: This is dismissive and does not assess risk.

steps.q: Among these clients, who is the SAFETY priority?

opts.text: A client whose voices are commanding him to harm someone and who says he is not sure he can resist
opts.rat: Command hallucinations to harm others with uncertain ability to resist is an immediate safety emergency taking top priority.

opts.text: A client with flat affect sitting quietly alone
opts.rat: Negative symptoms without a safety threat are lower acute priority.

opts.text: A client asking when the next group meets
opts.rat: A routine question is not a safety priority.

opts.text: A client who wants help writing a letter
opts.rat: This is a low-priority, non-urgent request.

steps.q: A client with schizophrenia genuinely does not believe he is ill, even after relapse. This lack of insight (anosognosia) is best understood as:

opts.text: A feature of the illness itself, not simple stubbornness—affecting willingness to take medication
opts.rat: Anosognosia is a symptom in which the person truly cannot recognize their illness; it strongly affects adherence and is approached with understanding, not blame.

opts.text: Proof the client is just being difficult on purpose
opts.rat: Lack of insight is a symptom, not deliberate difficulty.

opts.text: A sign the client is fully recovered
opts.rat: It does not indicate recovery; it reflects impaired insight.

opts.text: Unrelated to medication adherence
opts.rat: Poor insight is a major driver of medication nonadherence.

steps.q: A client repeatedly relapses after stopping oral antipsychotics. Which treatment approach is often used to support adherence?

opts.text: A long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic given on a schedule
opts.rat: LAIs provide medication over an extended period, reducing the risk of missed daily doses and relapse in clients who struggle with oral adherence.

opts.text: Stopping all medication permanently
opts.rat: Stopping medication increases relapse risk, the opposite of the goal.

opts.text: Doubling the missed doses when the client remembers
opts.rat: Adjusting doses is not the technician's role and is not the strategy; LAIs support adherence.

opts.text: Leaving adherence entirely to chance
opts.rat: Supporting adherence is important; LAIs are one tool for that.

steps.q: Which change should the technician report as a possible early sign of RELAPSE (decompensation) in a client with psychosis?

opts.text: Increasing withdrawal, poorer self-care, disrupted sleep, and appearing to respond to internal stimuli again
opts.rat: A return of withdrawal, declining self-care, sleep disturbance, and responding to internal stimuli can signal decompensation and should be reported.

opts.text: Improved grooming and active participation in groups
opts.rat: These are signs of improvement, not relapse.

opts.text: Sleeping and eating normally
opts.rat: Normal sleep and appetite are reassuring.

opts.text: Calm, coherent conversation
opts.rat: Coherent conversation suggests stability, not relapse.

steps.q: A client with psychosis tends to interpret language very literally (concrete thinking). The technician should:

opts.text: Communicate in clear, concrete terms and avoid idioms or abstract expressions
opts.rat: Concrete, literal communication prevents confusion for a client who cannot easily interpret figurative language.

opts.text: Use lots of idioms like 'hop to it' and 'break a leg'
opts.rat: Figurative expressions can be misunderstood by a concrete thinker.

opts.text: Speak in complex abstract metaphors
opts.rat: Abstract language increases confusion.

opts.text: Assume the client understands sarcasm
opts.rat: Sarcasm is easily misinterpreted by a concrete thinker.

steps.q: An acutely psychotic client becomes frightened and agitated, appearing to respond to threatening voices. The BEST approach is to:

opts.text: Stay calm, reduce stimulation, give the client space, and use a quiet, non-threatening manner
opts.rat: A calm, low-stimulation, non-threatening approach helps de-escalate fear-driven agitation and keeps everyone safe.

opts.text: Crowd close and speak loudly to get attention
opts.rat: Crowding and loudness increase fear and agitation.

opts.text: Argue that the voices are not real
opts.rat: Arguing escalates distress; presence and calm are more effective.

opts.text: Grab the client to move them quickly
opts.rat: Sudden physical contact can frighten and escalate a psychotic, fearful client.

steps.q: A client states with certainty, 'I am a powerful ruler and everyone must obey me' (a grandiose delusion). The BEST response is to:

opts.text: Avoid arguing or agreeing; acknowledge the feeling, gently focus on reality, and ensure safety
opts.rat: Neither confronting nor reinforcing the delusion is therapeutic; acknowledging the underlying feeling and redirecting to reality is appropriate.

opts.text: Agree and address the client as 'Your Majesty'
opts.rat: Playing along reinforces the delusion.

opts.text: Argue and prove the client is wrong
opts.rat: Arguing tends to entrench the delusion and damage trust.

opts.text: Laugh at the client's belief
opts.rat: Ridicule is nontherapeutic and harmful.

steps.q: A client is convinced his internal organs are rotting away, despite normal findings (a somatic delusion). The technician should:

opts.text: Acknowledge the client's distress without confirming the belief, and report the concern
opts.rat: Validating the distress (not the false belief) maintains trust; reporting allows the team to address it.

opts.text: Confirm that the organs are indeed rotting
opts.rat: Confirming a delusion reinforces it and is untrue.

opts.text: Tell the client he is being ridiculous
opts.rat: This is dismissive and nontherapeutic.

opts.text: Ignore the statement entirely
opts.rat: The distress is acknowledged and reported, not ignored.

steps.q: Which coping strategy can help a client manage distressing auditory hallucinations?

opts.text: Engaging in an activity, listening to music, or talking with someone to refocus attention
opts.rat: Purposeful engagement and distraction techniques can reduce the intensity and distress of hallucinations.

opts.text: Isolating in a dark, silent room to focus on the voices
opts.rat: Isolation and focusing on the voices tend to worsen distress.

opts.text: Encouraging the client to obey the voices
opts.rat: Encouraging obedience to hallucinations is dangerous.

opts.text: Telling the client to try harder to make them stop
opts.rat: This is unhelpful; practical coping strategies are more effective.

steps.q: Near a client with paranoid ideation, staff should AVOID:

opts.text: Whispering or laughing where the client can see but not hear, which can feed suspicion
opts.rat: Whispering or laughing nearby can be misread as plotting, increasing paranoia; open, transparent behavior builds trust.

opts.text: Speaking openly and clearly with the client
opts.rat: Open, clear communication is appropriate and builds trust.

opts.text: Being consistent and honest
opts.rat: Consistency and honesty are exactly what help a paranoid client.

opts.text: Explaining what they are about to do
opts.rat: Explaining actions reduces suspicion and is appropriate.

steps.q: When approaching a suspicious, guarded client, the technician should:

opts.text: Approach from the front, announce themselves, allow personal space, and ask before any touch
opts.rat: A visible, announced approach with respect for personal space and warning before touch reduces threat perception and keeps interactions safe.

opts.text: Approach quietly from behind to avoid startling
opts.rat: Approaching from behind can startle and frighten a paranoid client.

opts.text: Stand very close and touch the client without warning
opts.rat: Invading space and unexpected touch can feel threatening and escalate the client.

opts.text: Corner the client to hold their attention
opts.rat: Cornering increases fear and the risk of a defensive reaction.

steps.q: To help a client with prominent negative symptoms (such as low motivation), the technician should:

opts.text: Encourage small, gradual, achievable steps toward participation without overwhelming the client
opts.rat: Breaking activity into small, manageable steps supports engagement without overloading a client whose motivation and energy are impaired.

opts.text: Demand full participation in every activity at once
opts.rat: Overwhelming demands can increase withdrawal.

opts.text: Label the client as lazy and leave them alone
opts.rat: This misattributes symptoms and abandons the client.

opts.text: Do nothing, since negative symptoms cannot be helped
opts.rat: Gradual encouragement and structure can help; giving up is not appropriate.

steps.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops restlessness and an inability to sit still. The technician should recognize this could be:

opts.text: Akathisia (a medication side effect) rather than psychiatric agitation, and report it for evaluation
opts.rat: New motor restlessness on an antipsychotic may be akathisia, a side effect; distinguishing it from psychiatric agitation matters, so it is reported.

opts.text: Definitely just the client being difficult
opts.rat: Restlessness may be a medication side effect, not willful behavior.

opts.text: Something to ignore since it is harmless
opts.rat: Akathisia is distressing and is reported for evaluation.

opts.text: A reason to restrain the client immediately
opts.rat: Restraint is not the response; the possible side effect is reported.

steps.q: A paranoid client refuses medication because he fears it is poison. The BEST approach is to:

opts.text: Use a calm, consistent, trustworthy approach, avoid forcing, and report the refusal to the nurse
opts.rat: Building trust through consistency and honesty, not force, and reporting the refusal supports adherence over time while respecting the client.

opts.text: Force the medication into the client immediately
opts.rat: Forcing medication is unsafe, can be battery, and destroys trust.

opts.text: Threaten the client to make him comply
opts.rat: Threats are coercive and nontherapeutic (and can constitute assault).

opts.text: Secretly hide the medication in food without an order
opts.rat: Covert medication without appropriate authorization is improper and violates the client's rights.

steps.q: During a care task, a client keeps pausing and appears to be listening to something no one else hears. The technician should:

opts.text: Gently refocus the client on the present task and reality, and note/report the behavior
opts.rat: Calmly reorienting the client to the here-and-now supports functioning, and the observation is documented and reported.

opts.text: Ask the client to describe the voices in detail for entertainment
opts.rat: This is not therapeutic and can reinforce engagement with the hallucination.

opts.text: Pretend to hear the voices too
opts.rat: Pretending to share the hallucination is dishonest and reinforces it.

opts.text: Scold the client for not paying attention
opts.rat: Scolding is nontherapeutic; gentle refocusing is appropriate.

steps.q: The reality-based way to respond to a client's fixed false belief (delusion) is to:

opts.text: Not argue or agree—acknowledge it feels real to the client while calmly conveying your own different reality
opts.rat: Statements like 'I understand it seems real to you; I don't see it that way' present reality without attacking the client or reinforcing the delusion.

opts.text: Insist repeatedly that the belief is stupid
opts.rat: Attacking the belief damages trust and rarely changes it.

opts.text: Enthusiastically agree with the delusion
opts.rat: Agreeing reinforces the delusion.

opts.text: Demand the client prove the belief
opts.rat: Debating the delusion is not therapeutic.

steps.q: A client relapsed after stopping his medication and is embarrassed. The technician should:

opts.text: Respond nonjudgmentally and supportively, encouraging re-engagement with treatment
opts.rat: A nonjudgmental, supportive stance helps the client return to care rather than feel shamed and disengage.

opts.text: Scold the client for stopping the medication
opts.rat: Scolding shames the client and discourages re-engagement.

opts.text: Tell the client the relapse is entirely his own fault
opts.rat: Blame is nontherapeutic; support and re-engagement are the goal.

opts.text: Refuse to help until the client apologizes
opts.rat: Withholding help is inappropriate and unsafe.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in caring for a client with psychosis is to:

opts.text: Use calm reality-based communication, prioritize safety (especially command hallucinations), recognize relapse, support adherence, and report—without arguing or reinforcing delusions
opts.rat: The technician communicates supportively in reality, keeps the client and others safe, watches for relapse, supports treatment, and reports, while avoiding both confronting and reinforcing delusions.

opts.text: Argue clients out of their delusions
opts.rat: Arguing is nontherapeutic and ineffective.

opts.text: Reinforce hallucinations and delusions to build rapport
opts.rat: Reinforcing psychotic experiences is harmful, not rapport-building.

opts.text: Ignore command hallucinations about harm
opts.rat: Command hallucinations about harm are a top safety concern that must be addressed.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care (psychosis/schizophrenia care) — Phase-2 depth/application. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: negative symptoms and their misattribution; command-hallucination safety assessment and prioritization; anosognosia (lack of insight) and its effect on adherence; long-acting injectable antipsychotics as an adherence support; early signs of relapse/decompensation; concrete communication; de-escalating fear-driven agitation; responding to grandiose and somatic delusions without arguing or reinforcing; coping strategies for hallucinations; avoiding paranoia-feeding behaviors; safe approach to a guarded client; gradual engagement for negative symptoms; distinguishing akathisia (a medication side effect) from psychiatric agitation; supportive handling of medication refusal and relapse; and reality-based responses to delusions. Specific drug names, doses, and injection intervals are NOT asserted (antipsychotic classes/administration are covered in mh-core-06/10). Builds on and does not duplicate the foundational psychosis items in mh-core-02. Pending faculty review.
